title: Philip Watches Alexander Tame Bucephalus
text:
Plutarch tells this story in his Life of Alexander. A horse dealer from Thessaly named Philonicus brought a horse called Bucephalus to King Philip of Macedon, asking thirteen talents for him, an enormous price. When they took him out to the field to try him, the horse was wild. He reared up and would not let any of the king's men mount him or even speak to him. They were leading him away as useless.

The young Alexander, standing by, kept saying what a fine horse they were losing for lack of skill and nerve. At first Philip ignored him. Then he asked whether Alexander was criticizing his elders as if he knew better. Alexander said he could handle this horse better than they had. Philip asked what he would forfeit if he failed. The price of the horse, said Alexander, and everyone laughed.

Alexander had noticed that the horse was frightened of his own shadow. He turned him to face the sun, stroked him, let him run forward a little, then quietly slipped off his cloak and leapt onto his back. Without whip or spur, he let him go at full speed, and brought him back in triumph. The company cheered. Philip, Plutarch says, wept with joy and kissed his son, saying: "My son, seek a kingdom equal to yourself, for Macedonia is too small for you."

Plutarch adds that Philip, seeing his son could be led by reason but not forced, then sent for Aristotle to teach him.
lesson: Watching closely what a child can do, and recognizing it, gives confidence nothing else can. Children who can be reasoned with should be persuaded, not commanded.
people: Philip II of Macedon, Alexander the Great, Philonicus
